headline: Would have provided fiscal year 2016 funding for most U.S. military activities, but the Senate did not take it up and it did not become law.
what_it_does: The bill would have provided FY2016 money for the Department of Defense, including military pay, operations, weapons buying, research, and war-on-terrorism operations overseas. It would have raised total defense funding compared with FY2015 and set a 2.3% basic pay increase for military personnel. It also contained many limits on how the money could be spent, such as rules on buying American-made goods, transfers between accounts, and detainees at Guantanamo Bay.

who_it_affects.how: They would have received a 2.3% basic pay increase and funding for pay, housing allowances, and other personnel costs.
Their funding for operations, equipment, and personnel would have been set, and certain cuts to technician positions and Guard end strength would have been restricted.
They would have had to meet rules such as Buy American requirements for steel, bearings, and some ship parts, and rules on contractor bonuses and nondiscrimination claims.

who_it_affects.group: Military families and veterans' health care users
who_it_affects.how: Funding for Fisher Houses and the Defense Health Program would have been set, though the Defense Health Program base funding would have been reduced compared with FY2015.
Funds would have been barred from being used to move most non-citizen detainees into the United States or to modify U.S. facilities to hold them.
Certain contracting incentives and conveyances of excess Air Force housing units would have been provided to tribes in several western and midwestern states.
